concepts.name: Constitutional Qualifications for Presidential Candidacy (Article 58)
key_dimensions: Exhaustive list: citizen of India, age 35+, eligible for Lok Sabha membership — no additional qualifications can be imposed by law
UPSC trap: qualification is 'eligible for election as member of Lok Sabha' NOT 'must be a member of Lok Sabha'
Comparison with qualifications for Vice-President (Rajya Sabha eligibility) and Governor (different age bar does not apply)
Negative disqualifications embedded within Article 58(2): must not hold any office of profit under GoI, State, or any local authority

concepts.name: Office of Profit Disqualification for Presidential Candidate
key_dimensions: Article 58(2): A person holding an 'office of profit' under Union, State, or local/other authority is disqualified
Critical exception: Sitting President, Vice-President, Governor of any State, and Minister (Union or State) are NOT disqualified despite holding offices — statutory carve-out
UPSC trap: The exception covers 'Minister' but NOT Speaker/Deputy Speaker or members of Parliament — they must resign before contesting
Comparison with disqualification criteria under Article 102 (Lok Sabha membership) — overlap and distinction

concepts.name: Age Requirement: 35 Years and Its Implications
key_dimensions: Minimum age of 35 years — same as for Vice-President; contrast with 25 years for Lok Sabha and 30 years for Rajya Sabha
No maximum age limit for the President — UPSC frequently tests absence of upper age bar (contrast with Judges' retirement age)
Age must be completed on the date of nomination, not date of election — practical significance
Comparison with other constitutional functionaries: Governor (no age bar specified beyond citizenship), CAG, etc.

concepts.name: Citizenship Requirement for Presidential Candidacy
key_dimensions: Must be a 'citizen of India' — only natural or naturalised citizens qualify; Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) holders are ineligible
No provision for 'natural-born citizen' requirement unlike the US Constitution — any citizen including naturalised citizens can contest
Interaction with Citizenship Act 1955 and constitutional citizenship under Articles 5–11
UPSC angle: contrast with requirements for Prime Minister (no explicit citizenship clause in constitution — convention vs law)

concepts.name: Eligibility as Lok Sabha Member: Hidden Disqualifications
key_dimensions: Being 'eligible for election as member of Lok Sabha' imports all disqualifications under Articles 102 and Tenth Schedule by reference
Disqualifications under RPA 1951 (conviction, corrupt practices) automatically apply to presidential candidates
UPSC trap: A person disqualified for Lok Sabha under anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule) would also be ineligible for Presidency
Distinction: Lok Sabha membership requires name in electoral roll of any constituency — Presidential candidate need NOT be a registered voter (contested interpretation clarified by practice)

concepts.name: Nomination Process and Proposers/Seconders Requirement
key_dimensions: Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act 1952: candidate must have 50 proposers and 50 seconders from the Electoral College
Historical change: Originally only 10 proposers and 10 seconders were required — amended in 1997 to check frivolous candidates
Security deposit of ₹15,000 — forfeited if candidate fails to secure 1/6th of valid votes polled
UPSC angle: Proposers/seconders must be members of the Electoral College (elected MPs + elected MLAs) — nominated members cannot propose

concepts.name: The Electoral College for Presidential Election (Article 54)
key_dimensions: Composition: Elected members of both Houses of Parliament + Elected members of Legislative Assemblies of States AND Union Territories with legislatures (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K after reorganisation)
UPSC trap: Nominated members of Parliament and State Legislatures are EXCLUDED; Members of Legislative Councils (MLCs) are also EXCLUDED
Post 70th Amendment (1992): Electoral College includes elected members of UTs with legislatures — NCT of Delhi and Puducherry added
Comparison with Vice-Presidential election: Electoral College for VP = elected + NOMINATED members of both Houses (no state legislators) — critical distinction

concepts.name: Value of Votes in Presidential Election: Parity Formula
key_dimensions: Article 55(2): Value of each MLA's vote = Total population of state ÷ (Number of elected MLAs × 1000) — ensures parity between states
Value of each MP's vote = Total value of all MLA votes of all states ÷ Total number of elected MPs (both Houses)
Population used: 1971 Census figures — frozen by 84th Constitutional Amendment until 2026 (now extended to 2031 post-delimitation)
UPSC trap: MLAs of smaller states have lower individual vote value; MPs' vote value fluctuates with changes in state assembly strength

concepts.name: Single Transferable Vote and Proportional Representation in Presidential Election
key_dimensions: Article 55(3): Election by secret ballot using system of proportional representation by means of single transferable vote (STV)
Voter marks preferences (1, 2, 3…); a candidate must secure a quota = [Total valid votes ÷ (Number of seats + 1)] + 1
Significance: Ensures the President has broad consensus across parties and states — not just simple majority winner
UPSC angle: Compare with Vice-Presidential election (also STV + proportional representation) vs Lok Sabha election (first-past-the-post)

concepts.name: Term of Office: Five-Year Term Under Article 56
key_dimensions: Article 56(1): President holds office for 5 years from the date of entering upon office (not from date of election)
President continues to hold office even after expiry of 5 years until successor assumes charge — prevents constitutional vacuum
UPSC trap: Term is counted from date of 'entering upon office' — if swearing-in is delayed, term starts from swearing-in date, not election date
No limit on re-election — a person can be elected President any number of times (contrast with US: maximum 2 terms)

concepts.name: Re-election of the President: No Bar on Number of Terms
key_dimensions: Constitution places no restriction on re-election — Article 57 explicitly states a person who holds or has held office is eligible for re-election
Historical instance: Dr. Rajendra Prasad served two consecutive terms (1950–1962) — only President to do so
UPSC comparative angle: US President limited to 2 terms (22nd Amendment); India has no such bar — deliberate constitutional choice
Implication for continuity vs democratic rotation debate — relevant for essay/GS2 analytical questions

concepts.name: Oath or Affirmation of the President (Article 60)
key_dimensions: Administered by Chief Justice of India; in CJI's absence, the seniormost judge of Supreme Court available administers the oath
Content of oath: To faithfully execute the office AND to the best of ability preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and law
UPSC trap: President takes oath to 'preserve, protect and defend the Constitution' — this is stronger language than oath taken by Ministers (Article 75) who swear 'allegiance to Constitution'
Significance: Oath under Article 60 is the constitutional basis for President's power to send back Bills and act as constitutional guardian

concepts.name: Conditions of President's Office (Article 59): Prohibitions During Term
key_dimensions: Cannot be a member of either House of Parliament or any State Legislature — must vacate seat if elected while being a legislator
Cannot hold any other office of profit — ensures complete separation from other executive/legislative roles
Entitled to use official residence without payment of rent; emoluments, allowances, and privileges determined by Parliament
UPSC trap: Emoluments cannot be diminished during term of office (Article 59(3)) — same protection as judges; compare with Governor (Article 158)

concepts.name: Resignation of the President (Article 56(1)(a))
key_dimensions: President may resign by writing under hand addressed to the Vice-President — NOT to the Speaker or Prime Minister
Vice-President must immediately communicate the resignation to the Speaker of Lok Sabha
UPSC trap: Resignation of VP is addressed to President; resignation of President to VP — inverse relationship tested frequently
Historical context: No President of India has ever resigned — purely theoretical but constitutionally significant provision

concepts.name: Removal of President by Impeachment (Article 61)
key_dimensions: Ground: Violation of the Constitution — term is undefined/not elaborated in the Constitution (deliberate ambiguity)
Process: Charge initiated by either House; requires 14 days' notice signed by at least 1/4th of total membership of that House
Resolution to impeach must be passed by 2/3rd majority of total membership of the initiating House, then investigated and passed by 2/3rd of total membership of the other House

UPSC trap: Unlike judges' removal (requires address by Parliament), impeachment is a special procedure with 2/3rd of TOTAL MEMBERSHIP (not just members present and voting) — higher threshold; also President has right to appear and be represented

concepts.name: Comparison of Presidential Impeachment with Removal of Judges and Vice-President
key_dimensions: President: Article 61 — initiated in either House, 2/3rd of total membership of both Houses required, ground is 'violation of Constitution'

Supreme Court/High Court Judges: Article 124(4)/217 — initiated in either House, requires special majority (2/3rd present and voting + majority of total membership), ground is 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity'
Vice-President: Removed by resolution of Rajya Sabha passed by effective majority and agreed to by Lok Sabha — NO special majority, NO impeachment procedure
UPSC trap: No constitutional functionary (President, VP, Judges) can be removed by a simple majority — but the thresholds and procedures differ significantly

concepts.name: Discharge of Presidential Functions During Vacancy or Absence (Article 65 and 70)
key_dimensions: Article 65: Vice-President acts as President when office falls vacant (death, resignation, removal, inability) until new President is elected
Time limit for election of new President: Must be held within 6 months of vacancy arising — Article 62(2)
Article 70: Parliament may make provision for discharge of functions when neither President nor VP is available — currently Speaker of Lok Sabha acts (Presidential and VP's Act 1969)

UPSC trap: When VP acts as President, VP does NOT perform VP's functions (presiding over RS) — contrast with when VP merely 'performs functions' during temporary absence (then VP continues as RS Chairman)

concepts.name: Election Dispute Resolution in Presidential Election (Article 71)
key_dimensions: Article 71(1): All doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with election of President or VP shall be decided by Supreme Court — exclusive original jurisdiction
Article 71(3): The election of a person as President/VP cannot be challenged on the ground that the Electoral College was incomplete (e.g., vacancy in state legislature)
Supreme Court decision in Presidential election dispute is FINAL — no appeal lies; Election Commission of India has no role in Presidential elections
UPSC trap: SC acts as election tribunal for President/VP; for Parliament elections it is High Courts under RPA 1951, with SC in appellate jurisdiction — different forums

concepts.name: Salary, Emoluments, and Privileges of the President
key_dimensions: Charged on Consolidated Fund of India — not subject to vote of Parliament (ensures independence); current salary ₹5 lakh per month
Article 59(3): Emoluments and allowances cannot be varied to his disadvantage after election — protects during tenure
Post-retirement benefits: Former Presidents are entitled to pension, furnished accommodation, secretarial staff, medical facilities under Presidents' Emoluments and Pension Act 1951
UPSC angle: Compare with Governor's salary (charged on Consolidated Fund of State) and PM's salary (charged on Consolidated Fund of India as minister) — 'charged' vs 'voted' distinction

concepts.name: Immunity of the President from Legal Proceedings (Article 361)
key_dimensions: President is not answerable to any court for exercise and performance of powers and duties of office — complete immunity for official acts
No criminal proceedings can be instituted or continued against the President in any court during term of office
Civil proceedings: 2 months' notice must be given before filing suit against President in personal capacity — even for personal acts

UPSC trap: Immunity is NOT absolute for personal acts after leaving office; also, Article 361 does not bar judicial review of Presidential actions under Article 32/226 — the action can be challenged even if President is immune personally (landmark in Rameshwar Prasad case)
